chapter_theme: The body is impure: beneath skin, perfume and garlands it is a vessel of flesh, fluids and filth, and in death it is food for vultures and a grinning skull. Desire for a woman's body rests on not seeing this, and the renunciant who has seen it is not moved by the conventional praise of eyes and teeth.
structure_note: Quatrains 41-43 strip off the body's coverings, 44-45 give the renunciant's own refusal in parallel verses on eyes and teeth, 46-48 list what the body is and what becomes of it, and 49-50 let the skulls of the dead speak.

41.reading: The 'worthies' who cry 'O fair, lovely girl': do they not see the body's paltry dwelling? If skin the size of a fly's wing is torn from it, a stick is needed to drive away the crows.
41.nuance: Both commentators take புக்கில் as the body, a temporary lodging of the life; Pope renders it 'the heavenly home invisible'. Mudaliar notes that சான்றவர் (worthies) is used ironically for the petty-minded. The crows show how little stands between the admired body and carrion.

positions.position: The புக்கில் is the body itself, a lodging where the life stays for a while.
positions.quote: துச்சிலை-(உயிரானது ஒதுக்குக் குடியிருக்கும்) வீடாகிய உடம்பின் தன்மையை.

positions.position: The admirers do not know that the body is a paltry shelter.
positions.quote: உடம்பு அற்பமான ஓர் ஒதுக்கிடம் என்பதை அறியார் போலும் !

42.reading: If the body, full of openings beneath its skin, is handsome only through an outer covering that hides its falsity, then without speaking desire one should look at it as a bag turned inside out.
42.nuance: The commentators agree on the bag turned inside out; Pope instead renders பைம்மறி as 'an undeveloped embryo'. The verse asks for a change of viewpoint, not a change in the body.

positions.position: Look at the body as one looks at a bag turned so that the inside faces out.
positions.quote: பை மறியா-பையைப் போல,(உட்பக்கம் வெளிப் பக்கமாம்படி) மாற்றியதாக.

positions.position: Turn the body inside out like a bag and its truth becomes plain.
positions.quote: பையைத் திருப்பிப் பார்ப்பதுபோல் அவ்வுடலைத் திருப்பிப் பார்த்தால் உண்மை விளங்கும்.

43.reading: Will chewing fragrant spices, filling the head with flowers and putting on a false finery remove the foulness the great saw and abandoned, which is always strengthened by the work of eating?
43.nuance: Mudaliar takes மயல் as the impurities of a woman's body; Shanmuganar applies it to the body in general. The verse says only that the great saw it and gave it up.

44.reading: Shall I give way when blind and petty men trouble me by calling eyes water-lilies in clear water, darting carp or spears? I will go on my way having seen what an eye is: like a palm fruit scooped out once its water is drained.
44.nuance: The speaker is a renunciant guarding his resolve; the verse is personal resistance rather than general teaching. கண்ணில் (eyeless) turns the praisers' subject back on them.

45.reading: Shall I give way when untaught petty men chatter that smiles are jasmine buds and pearls? I will go on my way having seen the teeth and bones fallen and scattered in the burning ground for all to see.
45.nuance: A companion to 44 with the same frame; the evidence here is not anatomy but the cremation ground, so impurity and impermanence meet.

46.reading: Entrails, fat, blood, bone, linking sinews, skin, and flesh and grease set here and there: among these, which part is the woman with the fresh garland?
46.nuance: The question is a search for the person among the parts, and implies she is none of them; the verse uses the list, not argument, to dissolve the beloved.

47.reading: The fool calls out 'broad-shouldered one, bangle-wearer' to a pot that seeps filth from nine openings and churns with slime, because its covering of dark skin dazzles his eyes.
47.nuance: The terms of address the fool uses are the stock epithets of love poetry, so the verse aims at a literary convention as well as at desire.

48.reading: Those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing what the body is: have they not seen vultures, male and female, crowd in and tear at the stinking cart once its axle breaks?
48.nuance: Mudaliar reads the axle as the life and the cart as the body. The cart image recurs from 2, where wealth turned like a wheel.

49.reading: The skulls of the dead lying about, with deep sunken eye-holes that frighten those who see them, seem to laugh loudly and tell the living 'guard yourselves and keep to the path: this is what the body comes to'.
49.nuance: The speech is a poetic fancy, as Mudaliar notes (தற்குறிப்பேற்றம்). He names the path as renunciation; Shanmuganar names it as virtue.

50.reading: The white skulls of the dead, grinning so as to frighten, cure the infatuated of their fault; those so cured, seeing that this is the body's nature, do not count themselves as anything of worth.
50.nuance: Mudaliar takes the infatuated as men besotted with women and 'themselves' as their bodies; Shanmuganar takes it as the proud, cured of arrogance. The verse's own words allow both.

links.note: Both call the body a புக்கில், a lodging; Mudaliar even glosses with துச்சில், the Kural's word. The Kural uses it to show the life has no home of its own; the Naladiyar to show the body is a mean hut not worth desiring.
Kural 80 says a body without love is bone wrapped in skin, implying love makes it more. The Naladiyar treats every body as filth wrapped in skin and allows no such exception.
The water-lily as a figure for the eye appears in both. In Kural 1114 the lover says the lily would bow before her eyes; here the renunciant calls those who make that comparison eyeless.

Kural 1113's lover calls her teeth pearls and her eyes spears; this quatrain calls those who praise teeth as pearls untaught and petty, and answers with bones in the burning ground. The conflict holds if the Kural's Book of Love is read as valuing the lover's praise, not only as dramatised speech.
Kural 913 likens the embrace of women who sell themselves to embracing a corpse in the dark; the Naladiyar extends the corpse to every admired body, which the Kural does not.
In both the skulls laugh and teach: in 49 they speak to all the living, in 50 they cure the infatuated in particular.
Both conclude that the body is not worth valuing: for those ending births even the body is excess in Kural 345, and those cured by the skulls here count themselves as nothing.

new_concepts.gloss: the body, as a perishable and impure frame
new_concepts.label_source: The verses use யாக்கை (18, 27, 28, 30, 34) and the chapter title யாக்கை நிலையாமை.

source_issues: Quatrain 44: Shanmuganar's field also contains the text of quatrain 45 and his commentary on it, which is repeated under 45.
Quatrain 41: Mudaliar glosses துச்சிலை where the printed verse reads புக்கிலை, suggesting a variant text.
Quatrain 45: the Tamil has misprints, விடுவெனோ for விடுவேனோ and வேன3 for வேன்.
Quatrain 46: Mudaliar glosses எத்திறத்தான் (masculine) where the verse reads எத்திறத்தாள்.
Quatrain 50: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter, and its opening is garbled (கண்டார் அஞ் நகைத்து).
